statistical-thinking: Start with a clear question, a well-defined group, and a careful look at the data. Learn how averages, spread, charts and unusual values describe what happened—without confusing description with explanation or cause.
probability: See how probability describes uncertain events and how samples help us learn about a wider population. Work through conditional probability, Bayes’ rule, surveys and economic outcomes, while learning why rare events and biased samples change what a result means.
distributions: A distribution shows the values data can take; a sampling distribution shows how a summary such as an average would vary across samples. Explore why averages often become more stable, and where small samples, dependence and changing conditions make simple rules unreliable.
estimation: Use a sample to estimate a population quantity, then show how uncertain that estimate is. Learn why sample size, variation and the way data are collected shape a confidence interval—and why a precise estimate can still be biased or aimed at the wrong group.
p-values: Test a specific claim against a stated model and learn what a p-value measures: how surprising the data would be if that model were true. Put it alongside effect size, uncertainty and study design; a value below 0.05 is not proof, practical importance or the chance that a claim is false.
regression: Regression summarizes how an outcome changes with one or more measured factors, while accounting for the other factors included in the model. Learn to interpret coefficients and predictions, check how well a model fits, and see why a relationship is not automatically a cause—with examples such as wages, prices and policy outcomes.
causal: Causal inference asks what would have happened to the same people, places or firms under a different policy or treatment. Compare experiments and observational designs, use counterfactual reasoning, and identify the assumptions needed before a difference between groups can be called an effect.
time-series: Time series follow an economy or market across dates—for example, inflation, unemployment, output or prices. Learn to spot trends, persistence and changing volatility, make and assess forecasts, and distinguish predicting a movement from explaining what caused it.
returns-risk: Use investment returns as one practical example of change over time, compounding and variation. Work out how gains and losses combine, compare common risk summaries, and see why historical averages or volatility alone cannot guarantee what happens next.
portfolio: The risk of a group of investments depends not only on each asset’s ups and downs, but also on how they move together. Use covariance and correlation to understand diversification, then carry the same ideas to risks shared across firms, regions or other economic outcomes.
bayesian: Bayesian statistics combines an initial set of assumptions with new evidence to update uncertainty. Learn how prior beliefs and data contribute to a posterior distribution, then use simulation to carry uncertainty through a model—without treating a prior as something data cannot change.
backtesting: A backtest tries a rule on past data, but searching many possibilities can make random patterns look impressive. Learn how data leakage, selection, transaction costs and changing conditions affect historical results, and how to test a claim without reusing the same data as proof.
correlation: Correlation measures how strongly two numerical variables move together in a straight-line pattern. Explore scatterplots, covariance and the influence of unusual values, and learn why correlation alone cannot establish cause, rule out nonlinear links or guarantee future behaviour.
exploratory-data-analysis: Explore a dataset before choosing a model: check definitions, missing values and units, then use tables and charts to see patterns and unusual records. Build a repeatable first-pass workflow that can reveal data-quality problems without mistaking a chart for an explanation.
kernel-density: Kernel density estimation draws a smooth curve to summarize where observations are concentrated, without relying on fixed histogram bins. Compare smoothing settings to see how too much or too little smoothing can hide peaks, exaggerate noise and change the apparent tails.
statistical-tools: Learn the practical steps behind a trustworthy analysis: organise a dataset, check variable types and missing values, calculate summaries, and make clear charts. Use spreadsheets and introductory Python to keep the work reproducible, so results can be checked and updated.
research-design: Turn a broad economic question into a specific outcome, comparison, population and time period before estimating anything. Learn to define the effect you want to measure, choose a design that creates a credible comparison, and state assumptions and checks clearly.
experimental-design: Random assignment can make groups offered a programme and groups not offered it comparable on average. Learn what the effect of an offer means, how take-up and missing follow-up complicate results, and why findings from one trial may not apply everywhere.
iv-2sls: Instrumental variables use an outside source of variation—such as a rule or policy change—to study a factor that is difficult to compare directly. Learn the conditions an instrument must meet, how two-stage least squares uses it, and whose effect an estimate may represent.
difference-in-differences: Difference-in-differences compares how outcomes change over time in a policy group and a comparison group. Learn the key assumption that their outcomes would otherwise have followed similar trends, how event-study charts help assess timing, and why different policy timing can complicate the result.
regression-discontinuity: Regression discontinuity uses a cutoff in a policy rule—such as an eligibility score—to compare units just above and below it. See how different assignment rules work, check whether people can manipulate the score, and understand why the result usually applies only near the cutoff.
panel-fixed-effects: Panel data track the same people, firms or regions over time, helping separate lasting differences from changes within a unit. Learn how fixed effects and first differences work, what they cannot control for, and why repeated observations must be handled carefully.
robust-clustered-inference: A standard error describes how much an estimate might vary, but the right calculation depends on how data were collected, assigned and grouped. Learn when robust or clustered methods are useful, why groups—not just rows—can determine precision, and how few independent groups limit confidence.
matching-weighting: Matching and weighting make programme and comparison groups more alike on measured characteristics, such as earlier earnings or age. Learn to check whether the groups overlap and are balanced, understand propensity scores, and make clear that unmeasured differences can still distort a causal claim.
synthetic-control: When one region or institution adopts a policy, synthetic control builds a comparison by weighting similar places that did not. Learn to judge how well the comparison matched before the policy, which places contribute to it, and what placebo checks can—and cannot—show about a single case.
limited-outcomes: Many economic outcomes are not unrestricted numbers: employment is yes or no, clinic visits are counts, and spending may be zero for many people. Learn which models fit these patterns and how to report results as probabilities, expected counts or amounts people can interpret.
selection-missing-data: Missing values and dropouts are not just blank cells; they can change who the data represent and what a result measures. Learn to trace why observations are absent, how selection and attrition can bias an estimate, and which comparisons or sensitivity checks may help.
heterogeneous-effects: An average effect can hide very different outcomes for different people or places. Learn how subgroup and quantile analyses describe variation across groups or across the outcome distribution, and why searching many subgroups can produce patterns that are not reliable.
functional-form-specification: Models simplify the real world, and the shape of that simplification matters. Explore when relationships may be curved or depend on several factors together, how units and plots guide model choices, and how to check whether another reasonable specification changes the conclusion.
applied-macro-time-series: Use time-series tools to study inflation, unemployment, output and interest rates. Learn how trends and persistence shape forecasts, how shocks may unfold over time, and why predicting a movement is different from proving what caused it.
multilevel-partial-pooling: Data often come in groups—students in schools, workers in regions or patients in clinics—and small groups can look unusually high or low by chance. Compare one shared estimate, separate group estimates and partial pooling, which balances local information with the overall pattern.
complex-survey-sampling: A national survey is rarely a simple random sample: it may select households in stages, divide them into groups and sample some populations more often. Learn how weights, strata and clusters help produce population-relevant estimates, and how the survey design affects uncertainty.
survival-duration-analysis: Duration analysis studies how long it takes for an event—such as finding work, leaving school or recovering—to happen. Learn how to use follow-up that ends before the event, account for incomplete observations, and describe event rates without treating unfinished cases as failures.
spatial-dependence-regional-econometrics: Outcomes in nearby areas often resemble each other because people, jobs and policies cross local boundaries. Learn how to define neighbourhoods and measure spatial patterns, and distinguish geographic association from evidence that one area’s change caused a change in another.
bootstrap-inference: Bootstrap inference estimates how much a statistic may vary by repeatedly resampling the data already collected. See how to form standard errors and intervals, choose the right resampling unit for people, places or time periods, and why resampling cannot fix biased data.
statistical-power-planning: Power planning asks whether a study is likely to detect an effect large enough to matter, given its design and sample. Learn how effect size, outcome variation, clustering and attrition affect the numbers—and why a large sample cannot rescue a weak comparison.
measurement-error-economics: Economic concepts such as income, job access or working hours are observed through surveys, records or proxies that may be imperfect. Learn how measurement error can distort estimates, why its effects depend on what was measured, and how validation and repeated measurements can help.
price-indices-real-values: A price index summarizes how the cost of a defined basket changes over time; it is not a price tag that applies equally to everyone. Learn how basket weights and base periods work, calculate inflation, and adjust wages or spending to compare purchasing power.
regularization-cross-validation: When an economic prediction model has many overlapping predictors, a perfect fit to the historical sample may be a poor guide to the next month. Learn why Ridge and LASSO deliberately shrink coefficients, how cross-validation chooses tuning strength, and how to guard against leakage. An interactive synthetic lab lets you vary the penalty, predictor correlation and sample size while watching training and validation error move. The module also separates predictive success from causal evidence: a model that predicts unemployment well does not, by itself, identify what a policy would change.
meta-analysis-evidence-synthesis: A policy can be evaluated in many places and periods, producing a set of estimates rather than one decisive study. Learn how meta-analysis combines comparable effect estimates using their precision, why between-study differences call for a random-effects perspective, and how meta-regression relates effects to study features. The interactive forest-plot lab generates a clearly labelled synthetic evidence set and compares fixed- and random-effects summaries. The lessons also cover publication bias, multiple estimates from the same study, transparent inclusion rules and why counting significant results is not a substitute for synthesis.
causal-mediation-mechanisms: A programme may change an outcome because it changes an intermediate behaviour, but observing that behaviour does not automatically reveal a causal mechanism. Learn to distinguish total, direct and indirect effects, draw the treatment–mediator–outcome path, and state the assumptions needed to interpret mediation estimates. An interactive linear teaching model lets you vary the pathway and a hypothetical unmeasured mediator–outcome bias. The module explains why randomizing the programme does not randomize the mediator, why the familiar product-of-coefficients is limited, and how sensitivity analysis makes hidden-confounding assumptions visible.
partial-identification-bounds: When the data and credible assumptions cannot support one exact causal number, they may still rule out large parts of the answer space. Learn the difference between point identification and an identified set, derive worst-case bounds for binary outcomes with incomplete follow-up, and see how additional assumptions narrow a set at a cost. An interactive grant-evaluation lab recomputes lower and upper treatment-effect bounds as response rates and observed outcomes change. It distinguishes identification uncertainty from sampling uncertainty and warns against treating a bound midpoint as if it were a point estimate.
